titleStmt.title: Electoral Institutions and Legislative Behavior: Explaining Voting Defection in the European Parliament
titleStmt.author: Simon Hix

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Electoral Institutions and Legislative Behavior: Explaining Voting Defection in the European Parliament

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The results reveal that national parties are more able to enforce their wishes on their MEPs in systems containing electoral institutions that provide these principals with strong controls—specifically, in systems with closed-list proportional representation, small districts, or centralized candidate selection.

span.label: legislative voting defection
span.quote: Section III proposes a theory of legislative voting in the European Parliament that predicts the circumstances under which an MEP will defect from her parliamentary party or her national party.

span.label: observational-study
span.quote: To explain these MEP defection decisions and to test the predictions of the theoretical model, we can estimate the following fixed-effects logit model:

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Centralized candidate selection gives the national leadership a credible power to punish, so the MEP anticipates the cost and complies with national instructions
span.quote: Following the previous discussion, we can assume that the more centralized the system of candidate selection in the hands of the national party leadership, the more likely it is that the national party will be able to punish that MEP, regardless of the type of electoral system or the size of the MEP's electoral district.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The MEP weighs the cost of defecting from each principal and votes for whichever side leaves her better off, an expected-utility calculation
span.quote: Accordingly, each MEP makes a vote decision based on the overall expected utility of her action.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Where individual candidate votes decide electoral fortunes, reelection-seeking legislators cultivate a personal following independent of the party, which loosens party discipline
span.quote: In systems in which votes cast for individual candidates—as opposed to votes cast for a party list—significantly influence each candidate's electoral fortunes, legislators seeking reelection have strategic incentives to cultivate personal support among the electorate.

span.label: Statistical significance is inflated by the very large number of vote-decision observations.
span.note: what this limits: every significance claim in the paper: THE EFFECT OF MOST OF THE INDEPENDENT VARIABLES IS HIGHLY SIGNIFICANT, PRIMARILY BECAUSE OF THE LARGE NUMBER OF OBSERVATIONS
span.quote: The effect of most of the independent variables is highly significant, primarily because of the large number of observations.

span.label: Policy conflict between an MEP's two principals is not observed directly but approximated by survey-based distance measures.
span.note: what this limits: the policy-conflict variables: THESE ARE PROXY MEASURES OF POLICY CONFLICT BETWEEN THE TWO PARTY PRINCIPALS, built from survey distances rather than observed
span.quote: These are proxy measures of policy conflict between the two party principals.

span.label: The party-group coefficients do not generalise to MEPs in the largest national delegations because of how the model is specified.
span.note: what this limits: the party-group results: BECAUSE OF THE STRUCTURE OF THE MODEL, THESE RESULTS ... APPLY ONLY TO THOSE MEPS WHO ARE NOT MEMBERS OF THE FIVE LARGEST NATIONAL DELEGATIONS
span.quote: However, because of the structure of the model, these results for the two main European party groups apply only to those MEPs who are not members of the five largest national delegations in these party groups.

span.label: One of the two policy-conflict predictors does not yield a clear result for national-party defection.
span.note: what this limits: the national-party defection result specifically: THE EFFECT OF THE EU-INTEGRATION POLICY DISTANCE ... IS LESS CLEAR
span.quote: The effect of the EU-integration policy distance between a national party and its European party group, however, is less clear.

span.label: A formal category is collapsed into a different one on the basis of how voters behave, not on the rule that defines it: semiopen-list systems are treated as closed-list because voters in practice choose the preordered list.
span.note: what this limits: the candidate-centred versus party-centred classification of electoral systems: semiopen-list systems are placed with closed-list ones because of observed voter behaviour rather than the rule
span.quote: In most countries employing these systems, however, the overwhelming majority of voters choose to vote for the preordered list rather than for individual politicians. Accordingly, votes for individual candidates rarely determine which candidates are elected. Therefore, because parties control who gets elected, most semiopen-list PR systems are, in practice, very similar to closed-list PR systems.

span.label: The key explanatory variable is measured by proxy, and the reason given is endogeneity rather than validity: the observed quantity would be caused by the thing being explained.
span.note: what this limits: the conflict variable as a measure of conflict in the vote at hand: it is a proxy, adopted because conflict observed in a particular vote is endogenous to the vote decisions being explained
span.quote: These are proxy measures of policy conflict between the two party principals. This, however, is preferable to using observed conflict in each vote because conflict in a particular vote is endogenous to the MEPs' vote decisions.

span.label: One side of the model is assumed non-strategic, and the assumption is adopted because the quantity involved is endogenous.
span.note: what this limits: the party group's behaviour in this model: it is assumed not to act strategically when issuing voting instructions, while the national party is allowed to
span.quote: because the size of internal conflict is endogenous to the party group majority's position on an issue, I assume that the party group does not act strategically when issuing voting instructions—the majority simply takes a position, which is then communicated to the backbenchers.

span.label: The arguments the article sets out to adjudicate are reported as never having been tested.
span.note: what this limits: the debate over a single European electoral system: the article states the existing arguments have remained normative and have not been developed theoretically or tested empirically
span.quote: However, these arguments have remained at a normative level and have not been developed theoretically or tested empirically.

span.label: The merged electoral-system class is a modelling decision resting on a behavioural generalisation - that parties control who gets elected, so voter preferences for individuals rarely matter - and every result for that class inherits it.
span.quote: Accordingly, votes for individual candidates rarely determine which candidates are elected. Therefore, because parties control who gets elected, most semiopen-list PR systems are, in practice, very similar to closed-list PR systems

span.label: a vector of 1,031 dummy variables, one for every vote
span.note: eliminates: that the estimate is driven by the differing defection rates and political salience of particular votes rather than by the electoral institution
span.quote: VOTE is a vector of 1,031 dummy variables that indicate each vote; these variables are included to control for the effect of varying levels of defection and political salience of each vote.

span.label: policy conflict
span.quote: These are proxy measures of policy conflict between the two party principals.

span.label: closed-list proportional representation
span.quote: At one end of the spectrum, closed-list proportional representation (PR) systems represent the most party-centered settings.

span.label: semiopen-list PR systems
span.quote: Some countries use semiopen- or ordered-list PR systems, in which parties propose preordered lists and voters can either vote for the party list as a whole or for an individual politician.

span.label: roll-call votes
span.quote: To test the theory, I collected the decisions of all MEPs in all roll-call votes taken during the first year of the 1999-2004 parliament.

span.label: closed-list
span.quote: Accordingly, votes for individual candidates rarely determine which candidates are elected. Therefore, because parties control who gets elected, most semiopen-list PR systems are, in practice, very similar to closed-list PR systems

span.label: electoral system - AS FORMAL RULE: semiopen- or ordered-list PR, where voters may vote for the list or for an individual politician
span.quote: Some countries use semiopen- or ordered-list PR systems, in which parties propose preordered lists and voters can either vote for the party list as a whole or for an individual politician.

span.label: electoral system - AS PRACTICE: the same systems classified with closed-list PR, because votes for individual candidates rarely decide who is elected
span.quote: Accordingly, votes for individual candidates rarely determine which candidates are elected. Therefore, because parties control who gets elected, most semiopen-list PR systems are, in practice, very similar to closed-list PR systems.

span.label: policy conflict - a PROXY measure between the two party principals, preferred over the conflict actually observed in a vote precisely because the observed version is endogenous
span.quote: These are proxy measures of policy conflict between the two party principals. This, however, is preferable to using observed conflict in each vote because conflict in a particular vote is endogenous to the MEPs' vote decisions.

span.label: policy conflict - measured by proxy ON PURPOSE: observed per-vote conflict is rejected as endogenous to the decision being explained, so the construct is measured away from the thing it predicts
span.quote: CONFL is a vector of two variables that indicates the level of policy conflict between an MEP's national party and her European party group on the two main dimensions of EU politics. These are proxy measures of policy conflict between the two party principals. This, however, is preferable to using observed conflict in each vote because conflict in a particular vote is endogenous to the MEPs' vote decisions

span.label: builds-on → Gabel and Hix (2002), "The European Parliament and Executive Politics in the EU"
span.quote: This builds on the model in Matthew Gabel and Simon Hix,

span.label: semiopen-list PR systems —same-as→ closed-list
span.note: differs in: NOTHING THAT MATTERS TO THE OUTCOME, WHICH IS THE POINT: the two are formally distinct - semiopen lists let voters express a preference for individuals - but 'because parties control who gets elected, most semiopen-list PR systems are, IN PRACTICE, very similar to closed-list PR systems'. The formal distinction survives; the behavioural one does not · strength of the relation: 0.8 — A FORMAL CATEGORY COLLAPSED INTO ANOTHER ON THE EVIDENCE OF PRACTICE, and the record already carries both readings as senses of `electoral system` - AS FORMAL RULE and AS PRACTICE. The analysis then treats the merged class as one, so every downstream coefficient depends on this move.
span.quote: Accordingly, votes for individual candidates rarely determine which candidates are elected. Therefore, because parties control who gets elected, most semiopen-list PR systems are, in practice, very similar to closed-list PR systems

span.label: policy conflict —operationalised-as→ roll-call votes
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE PROXY IS CHOSEN OVER THE DIRECT MEASURE FOR A STATED REASON, AND THE REASON IS ENDOGENEITY: the two variables are 'PROXY MEASURES of policy conflict … This, however, is PREFERABLE to using OBSERVED conflict in each vote because conflict in a particular vote is ENDOGENOUS to the MEPs' vote decision.' The observable quantity is rejected precisely because it is downstream of what is being explained - a rare case of a proxy defended rather than apologised for.
span.quote: CONFL is a vector of two variables that indicates the level of policy conflict between an MEP's national party and her European party group on the two main dimensions of EU politics. These are proxy measures of policy conflict between the two party principals. This, however, is preferable to using observed conflict in each vote because conflict in a particular vote is endogenous to the MEPs' vote decisions

span.label: logistic regression
span.quote: To explain these MEP defection decisions and to test the predictions of the theoretical model, we can estimate the following fixed-effects logit model:

span.label: fixed effects
span.quote: Fixed effects (dummy variables) for each of the 1,031 votes are included in all the models but are not reported.

span.label: predicted probability
span.quote: In logit analysis, this requires calculating the conditional probability of MEPs voting against their European party groups/national parties for different values of the independent variables.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: the figures in parentheses represent the difference in percent of the probabilities at the upper and lower limits of the 95 percent confidence interval

span.label: significance test

MEPs elected under institutions that weaken their national party's grip — a candidate-centered electoral system, decentralized candidate selection, and large district magnitude — are less likely to vote against their European party group.
span.quote: The less control a national party can exert over its MEPs as a result of the electoral institutions—if there is a candidate-centered electoral system, decentralized candidate selection, and a large district magnitude— the less likely it is that an MEP from this party will vote against the majority position of her European party group.

span.label: The same three institutions push in the opposite direction for the other principal: candidate-centered voting rules, decentralized candidate selection, or a large district each make an MEP more likely to vote against her own national party.
span.quote: In all models, if an MEP is elected under candidate-centered voting rules, with decentralized candidate-selection rules, or in a district with a large magnitude, that MEP is more likely to vote against her national party.

span.label: For defection from the national party the two institutions do not add up independently: only the combination of a candidate-centered system with decentralized selection raises defection, since either a party-centered system or centralized selection alone is enough to suppress it.
span.quote: An MEP is more likely to vote against her national party only when she is elected under a candidate-centered system with decentralized candidate-selection rules.

span.label: Longer service in the European Parliament lowers defection from the European party group but raises defection from the national party.
span.quote: Finally, as expected, the longer an MEP has been in the European Parliament, the less likely it is that she will vote against her European party group, but the more likely it is that she will vote against her national party;

span.label: Domestic constitutional design — semipresidentialism in France and federalism in Germany — does not carry over into MEP voting behaviour, since MEPs from both countries defect less than average from their national parties.
span.quote: Interestingly, the national party results suggest that the design of legislative-executive relations and the structure of territorial government at the domestic level does not affect individual legislative behavior in the European Parliament.

span.label: Defection is rare overall: MEPs almost always voted with the majorities of both their European party group and their national party.
span.quote: As predicted, most of the time, MEPs voted the same way as the majorities of both their European party group and national party did.

span.label: National parties enforce their voting instructions best where the rules give them strong control, namely closed-list PR, small districts, or centralized candidate selection; where the rules are open-list PR, large districts, or decentralized selection, MEPs side with their European party group instead.
span.quote: The results reveal that national parties are more able to enforce their wishes on their MEPs in systems containing electoral institutions that provide these principals with strong controls—specifically, in systems with closed-list proportional representation, small districts, or centralized candidate selection.

span.label: closed-list proportional representation (PR) system
span.quote: At one end of the spectrum, closed-list proportional representation (PR) systems represent the most party-centered settings. In these systems, parties present lists of candidates, and voters cannot influence the order of the candidates on them.

span.label: semiopen- or ordered-list PR system
span.quote: Some countries use semiopen- or ordered-list PR systems, in which parties propose preordered lists and voters can either vote for the party list as a whole or for an individual politician.

span.label: fully open-list PR system
span.quote: In fully open-list PR systems, candidates on each party's list are presented in no strategic order—for example, the candidates can be listed alphabetically—and voters must pick an individual candidate.

span.label: single-transferable-vote (STV) system
span.quote: Similarly, in STV systems, voters exercise ordinal preferences for the candidates in multimember constituencies.

span.label: electoral institutions (the three that shape politician-party relations)
span.term: electoral institutions (the three that shape politician-party relations)
span.quote: Three main electoral institutions shape the relationship between politicians and parties: the electoral system; district magnitude; and candidateselection rules.

span.label: an MEP's two principals
span.quote: We then assume that each MEP has two principals: her European parliamentary group and her national party.

span.label: voting defection (operational definition)
span.quote: if the majority of a party group voted yes, an MEP is considered to have defected from this group in a particular vote if she registered either a no or an abstain in the vote.

span.label: the European Parliament as a laboratory
span.term: the European Parliament as a laboratory
span.quote: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AS A LABORATORY The European Parliament is a good laboratory for isolating the impact of electoral institutions on individual legislative behavior.

span.label: electoral and candidate-selection institutions (vector EL_INST)
span.quote: Table 2 summarizes the independent variables' predicted effects on the dependent variables; the electoral institution variables should be in opposite directions for the two dependent variables.

span.label: Electoral System (candidate-centered vs party-centered)
span.quote: Electoral System is a dummy variable that indicates the electoral system under which an MEP is elected and takes a value of one if an MEP is elected under a candidate-centered system (either a fully open-list PR or STV system) and a value of zero if an MEP is elected under a party-centered system (either a closed- or semiopen-list PR system).

span.label: Candidate Selection (centralized vs decentralized)
span.quote: Candidate Selection is a dummy variable that indicates the candidate-selection rules under which an MEP is elected, and takes a value of one if an MEP is elected under centralized rules and a value of zero if an MEP is elected under decentralized rules.

span.label: District Magnitude
span.quote: District Magnitude is a continuous variable that measures the magnitude of a candidate's electoral district.

span.label: policy conflict between national party and European party group (Left-Right Distance, EU Integration Distance)
span.term: policy conflict between national party and European party group (Left-Right Distance, EU Integration Distance)
span.quote: By contrast, the policy conflict variables should have a similar directional effect on the two dependent variables.

span.label: MEP defection from her European party group / from her national party
span.term: MEP defection from her European party group / from her national party
span.quote: The model is estimated for two dependent variables: defection from a European party group, and defection from a national party.

span.label: seniority (length of time in the European Parliament)
span.term: seniority (length of time in the European Parliament)
span.quote: SEN is a control variable that takes into account the "seniority" of an MEP in the European Parliament.

span.label: European party group membership (EPP, PES)
span.quote: EPG is a vector of two dummy variables that controls for the effect of membership in the two largest party groups on MEP defection

span.label: national party delegation membership (ten largest delegations)
span.term: national party delegation membership (ten largest delegations)
span.quote: NP is a vector of ten dummy variables that controls for the effect of membership in the ten largest national party delegations (the main parties on the left and right in the five largest EU member states) on MEP defection.

span.label: individual roll-call vote (1,031 vote dummies)
span.quote: VOTE is a vector of 1,031 dummy variables that indicate each vote; these variables are included to control for the effect of varying levels of defection and political salience of each vote.

span.label: 1,031 — roll-call votes held in the European Parliament between July 1999 and June 2000, cast by 626 sitting MEPs, producing 645,406 individual vote decisions
span.quote: 1,031 rollcall votes took place between July 1999 and June 2000. In these votes, with 626 MEPs serving, there were 645,406 separate vote decisions.

span.label: 396,167 — vote decisions left in the analysis after exclusions, made by 526 MEPs from fifty-five national parties in fourteen member states
span.quote: Once these decisions were removed from analytical consideration, 396,167 vote decisions remained, by 526 MEPs (representing 82 percent of all MEPs serving during that period) from fifty-five national parties and fourteen member states

span.label: more than 30 percent — reduction in the probability of voting against one's European party group for an MEP elected under the full set of institutions granting independence from the national party
span.quote: An MEP chosen via institutions that afford her a high level of independence from her national party leadership is more than 30 percent less likely to vote against her European party group than an MEP elected under the alternative set of institutions.

span.label: approximately 20 percent — reduction in the probability of voting against one's national party for an MEP elected under the full set of institutions giving the national leadership control
span.quote: Conversely, an MEP chosen via institutions that provide a high level of control to her national party leadership is approximately 20 percent less likely to vote against her national party than an MEP elected under the alternative set of institutions.

span.label: 16 percent / 15 percent — EPP members are that much less likely, and PES members that much more likely, than the average MEP to vote against their European party group
span.quote: Controlling for the membership of the main national party delegations in the groups, members of the European People's Party are approximately 16 percent less likely to vote against their European party group than the average MEP, while members of the Party of European Socialists are 15 percent more likely to vote against their European party group.

span.label: 33 percent (± 2 percent) — extra likelihood that British Conservative MEPs vote against their European party group relative to the average MEP (Model 3); in Model 8 they are 19 percent (± 7 percent) more likely to defect from their national party
span.quote: In Model 3, for example, British Conservative MEPs are 33 percent (± 2 percent) more likely to vote against their European party group than the average MEP, and in Model 8 they are 19 percent (± 7 percent) more likely to defect from their national party.

span.label: 7,504 — double defections in which an MEP voted yes or no directly against both principals — under 2 percent of all analysed vote decisions
span.quote: However, only 7,504 of these double defections (comprising less than 2 percent of all MEP vote decisions during this period) represented cases in which MEPs expressed a directly opposing view from their party principals

span.label: One hundred ninety-five MEPs (31 percent of the 626 members) — respondents to the EPRG survey used to build the left-right and EU-integration policy-distance measures
span.quote: One hundred ninety-five MEPs (31 percent of the 626 members) completed the survey, and these returns constitute a good sample of the total population of MEPs.
